nameStory: Wild cherry gets its name from being the untamed ancestor of the sweet cherries we know from orchards and grocery stores. Originally from Europe and Asia, this tree earned the nickname 'gean' in some regions, from the Old French word meaning 'to bear fruit.' It's called 'wild' not because it's fierce, but because it grows freely in nature without human cultivation.
description: Wild cherry is a tall, graceful tree that can reach 50-80 feet high, creating an impressive canopy in the forest. It's part of the rose family, sharing relatives with apples, strawberries, and of course, other cherries. The tree produces clusters of white flowers in spring followed by small, dark red cherries that birds absolutely love. Its smooth, reddish-brown bark often peels in horizontal strips, giving the trunk a distinctive banded appearance.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy reddish-brown bark that peels off in horizontal strips like natural tape, revealing lighter bark underneath. Run your hand along it - it feels surprisingly smooth for a wild tree.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white flowers with five petals arranged in drooping clusters of 2-6 blooms. They have a sweet, almond-like fragrance that's especially noticeable on warm spring days.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with pointed tips and serrated edges, arranged alternately along branches. They feel slightly thick and have tiny red glands at the base where the leaf meets the stem.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round cherries that start green, turn bright red, then ripen to dark red or nearly black. They're sweet but often have a slightly bitter aftertaste compared to cultivated cherries.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall tree with a straight trunk and oval-shaped crown. Branches tend to grow upward at sharp angles, creating a somewhat narrow silhouette compared to spreading shade trees.

habitat: Wild cherry thrives in rich, well-drained soils along forest edges, in clearings, and sometimes in abandoned fields where it can get plenty of sunlight. You'll often find it mixed with maples, oaks, and other hardwoods in southern New England's deciduous forests. It prefers slightly acidic soil and doesn't tolerate wetlands or very sandy conditions.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters bloom in late April to May, filling the air with sweet fragrance and attracting bees and other pollinators. New leaves emerge bright green and slightly bronze-tinged.
seasonality.summer: Cherries ripen from green to dark red by mid to late summer, creating a feast for birds. The glossy green leaves provide dense shade and the distinctive bark is most visible.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant yellow to orange-red before dropping. The smooth, banded bark becomes more prominent as surrounding trees lose their leaves.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the tree's upright growth pattern, and the reddish-brown bark with horizontal peeling strips makes identification easy even without leaves.

funFact: Wild cherry bark was once so prized for cough medicine that it was literally worth its weight in silver to early pharmacists - the bark contains compounds that suppress coughing, and cherry cough drops today still try to mimic that original wild cherry flavor.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with black cherry, but wild cherry has smoother, more colorful bark that peels in obvious horizontal strips, while black cherry has darker, scaly bark. Memory trick: Wild cherry's bark looks 'wild' with its peeling strips, while black cherry's bark is 'black' and broken into scales.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - while the ripe fruit is delicious, all other parts of wild cherry (leaves, bark, seeds) contain compounds that can be toxic if consumed in large quantities. Birds can safely eat the whole fruit, but humans should stick to just the flesh and avoid the pits.
compareHints: Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters. Black cherry has darker, scaly bark and longer flower clusters, while chokecherry stays much smaller and has flowers in upright spikes. Fire cherry has similar peeling bark but is much smaller and has flowers in flat-topped clusters rather than drooping ones.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
